new_statements.rule_in_words: The position of word accent is unknown and unknowable from the ~100-word epigraphic corpus; the only inference is negative: final syllables show more vowel reduction (syncope) than other positions, so the accent was not word-final.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the whole statement is hedged ('nothing positive can be said'). Other sources add only implicit or speculative accent assumptions: Prósper 2004: 173 transcribes IFADEM as [i:'fadim] (penult) without a rule; Prósper & Villar 2009: 17, 29 speak of closing in 'sílaba átona' and syncope in -yom > -im; Vallejo 2013: 283 fn. 48 floats 'una diferencia acentual' (*ówila vs *dowíterus/*dowitérus) as one possible explanation for loss of -w-.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, inferred from historical vowel reduction in Latin-alphabet inscriptions (1st c. BCE-2nd c. CE); no living speakers, no citation forms, no phonetic evidence possible.
new_statements.identity_note: Lusitanian (lusi1235, ISO xls) is an extinct language known from four or five short Latin-alphabet inscriptions (Arroyo de la Luz I-III, Lamas de Moledo, Cabeço das Fráguas, Arronches; c. 100 words) plus onomastics; some authors (Prósper, Untermann) call the wider complex 'Lusitanian-Galician' (lusitano-galaico). Stifter 2018 describes the epigraphic language as a whole, no dialect distinction.
